searchText: This isn't an appropriate place to ask such questions. This is an Ethereum research and development server. I think now's the good time to discuss making this server invite-only I would personally prefer to avoid that. A large number of people who currently do "core dev" work got started by just casually following along. I would hate to cut that path off for people and require they commit a certain amount before they are even allowed to follow along. Plus, how would we determine who is allowed to join and who isn't? I think more moderators are needed in this case. Since we do not want to limit newcomers. An intermediate solution is to make a large part of channels read only and write by invitation. This way you reduce spam to just a few general channels that devs may choose to not follow. And those that have something to post can do so in those general channels until they get permission to write. I would bet that granting permission is a quick and easy task for moderators: it takes only one message to realize someone is off-topic or not <@!301186049323958275> Why didnt ethereum made a a system that can check that all parameters required are achieved before starting to make the transaction The state of the world may change between when the transaction is initially checked and when the transaction is eventually included. For example, if you are trading on a DEX, the price may change over time causing a transaction to become invalid, or become valid, or alternate back and forth. You can't know for sure what the world state the transaction executes against will be until you actually execute it at its final position in the blockchain. The system *does* do a bunch of validity checks on the transaction before passing it around via gossip, it doesn't just blindly accept everything. However, EVM execution specifically is delayed until final inclusion time, at which point the transaction has already cost the network in terms of gossip, storage, etc. so what is the differences between that to bitcoin? because the block time is longer? <@!301186049323958275> Bitcoin doesn't have state, it only has UTXOs. There isn't anything someone else can do that will cause a transaction that previously would have succeeded to fail. sry for being ignorant but UTXO you mean is the path of working by a spending ? and what does it mean state? <@!301186049323958275> Dyor Ethereum has global data storage, and people can write logic that is conditional on that storage. Bitcoin's only storage is UTXOs, which have very limited logic that can be applied to them and a transaction has limited visibility into UTXOs besides the ones it is spending from. Essentially, Bitcoin script can't do much besides transferring BTC, so it is *far* easier to make guarantees about transaction validity than on Ethereum. <@!301186049323958275> tyvm 🙂 <@!488328812501663744> I did but still didnt understand last question xD I read in ethereum page base fee is 100 so why is it changes with the time ? and why is it change ? I don't know where you read that. It is entirely automated/dynamic. why does it change? what are the reasons? the gas capacity? What people bid How full blocks are at the current gas fee changes the next block gas fee. This is a good line of questioning for <#692078615269212180>. 😄 (back where you started) Is there any info on attack v defence costs of creating fake nodes and requests to prevent genuine nodes from being able to sync? Or we assume existence of honest nodes that will serve unlimited number of requests? https://bitcoin.stackexchange.com/questions/61151/eclipse-attack-vs-sybil-attack Starting from that paper: https://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&as_sdt=2005&sciodt=0%2C5&cites=4560703012762650843&scipsc=1&q=eclipse&btnG= ty 🙂 ^^ its gas capacity in the end Thanks! Will read There's probably a whole lot of garbage between those papers, but hopefully something useful to you as well will see 🙂 Everyone is allowed. It's just an extra step to deter scammers and spam. A more elaborate captcha basically In my experience, spammers and scammers are more capable than actual humans at bypassing server join requirements. 🙂 Well, it does help in our case Erigon Discord is spam and scam free, exactly because ppl have to come knocking to one of the inviters first It can work for an exclusive community, where you are fairly picky about who you invite (need to know someone to get in). I don't think it scales to an open community though, where we want to encourage newcomers who don't have previous connections. I think such inclusivity is overrated At the end of the day, we get real contributors either by hire, or through word of mouth I don't believe average developer Joe can become a meaningful Ethereum contributor without either I don't think exclusive is an unreasonable choice for some organizations. I just don't think it is a good fit for Ethereum is all. I believe we *have* gained a number of positive contributors to Ethereum who didn't enter via hire or prior connections. It is of course hard to say of course how many would have found their way in anyway if the community was less open. Sometimes it starts with a lurker who sees a question they can answer after lurking for 6 months and that opens up a dialog that causes them to engage more and more over time. I'm not sure that the occasional lurker is really worth the whole openness charade Besides, there's an apprenticeship program now I don't think Ethereum's openness is a charade. _that_ is much more interesting in terms of efficiency The apprenticeship program itself is a closed system. 🙂 You can apply as a stranger, but if you don't get "accepted" for whatever reason, that doesn't necessarily mean you won't be able to contribute. I like having non-traditional paths to contributing to Ethereum besides "apply, pass interview, get hired". I think the traditional paths are very valuable as well of course, I just like having multiple routes. can do this ... even if all channels have free write access, there can be a consistent place to direct newcomers to - from where someone can further redirect based on need (support, scam, solidity, ethereum basics) ^ I've been reading the documentation on ethers.js and testing solidity contracts. For the life of me, I cannot find an example that deploys a contract and gives the contract ether in my tests. Does anyone know where I can read about doing that? I've tried doing it in the deploy function (but get an invalid argument count error, so the deploy function checks the constructor). And, doing something like ``` const [owner, addr1] = await ethers.getSigners(); params = { from: owner,to: addr1, value: ethers.utils.parseUnits(strEther, "ether").toHexString()}; const txHash = await owner.provider.sendTransaction(params); ``` results in ```Error: invalid hexlify value (argument="value", value={"from":"<SignerWithAddress 0xf39Fd6e51aad88F6F4ce6aB8827279cffFb92266>","to":"<SignerWithAddress 0x70997970C51812dc3A010C7d01b50e0d17dc79C8>","value":"0x1bc16d674ec80000"}, code=INVALID_ARGUMENT, version=bytes/5.4.0)``` Is there any provider (like infura or getblocks) who expose GraphQL endpoints?
